title: General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments

concept.text: The innovation would be a robot that can enter an unfamiliar ordinary home or small workplace, understand a requested task, and carry it through by moving and manipulating objects without the environment being redesigned for it. Its competence would extend across changes in objects, layouts, lighting, and instructions, including multi-step tasks where success depends on physical contact. The target is autonomous execution without demonstrations for each evaluation task or teleoperation during execution. This is a capability goal, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The central advance would connect understanding to dependable physical action. Recognizing an object or interpreting an instruction is insufficient if a robot fails when the object's placement, the wording, or the interaction dynamics change. Colosseum V2 documents this gap in evaluated robot policies and provides a framework for measuring generalization under visual, language, and action changes. The broader research goal also includes transfer across robot bodies, which is a separate challenge from using one robot successfully in many environments.

significance.text: As a conditional impact judgment, reliable autonomy of this kind would substantially expand where machines can perform useful physical work. Within a validated task range, a robot could handle household chores or small-workplace operations despite variation in rooms, objects, and task sequences. The revolutionary feature would be the ability to accommodate ordinary environments and their changes, reducing the need to prepare a special setting for each activity.

Sustained powered flight is a proposed analogy for the scale of the change: a machine gains a practically useful ability to operate in an environment that was not built around it. The analogy does not establish equivalent historical or economic impact. Nor does a proposed 90 percent task-success threshold establish reliability comparable to a careful person; the consequences and severity of the remaining failures matter.

Broader industrial deployment, laboratory automation, and remote physical presence are conditional downstream possibilities. They would require additional validation for particular equipment, materials, workflows, and operating conditions. Remote presence would also require suitable communications and interaction capabilities. A household demonstration would not by itself establish these applications, economy-wide labor replacement, theorem-proving competence, or the ability to replace every cognitive profession.

The technical basis for the opportunity includes combining physical skills into sustained activity. Colosseum V2 includes long-horizon manipulation composed of multiple primitive actions, alongside tasks involving insertion, tools, and articulated objects. These are relevant building blocks for useful work, but their inclusion in a benchmark does not demonstrate dependable deployment across ordinary homes or workplaces.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is robust perception-to-action generalization: maintaining successful behavior when the scene, instruction, or physical interaction differs from training. It must support sustained multi-step execution, where an early error can compromise later actions. In Colosseum V2, strong performance under baseline conditions does not imply strong generalization across visual, language, and action changes. This identifies limitations of the evaluated systems, without establishing that every existing system fails the full autonomy goal.

Contact-sensitive control remains a concrete barrier. The benchmark's rigid-body simulation does not capture deformable-object manipulation or the full complexity of frictional uncertainty, compliance, force feedback, and stick–slip transitions. These omissions matter when extending benchmark performance to activities involving cloth, flexible materials, or delicate and variable contact. A controller must cope with the physical interaction itself, beyond choosing a plausible action from visual and language inputs.

Engineering synthesis: hardware must supply the reach, mobility, dexterity, sensing, and actuation needed for the intended work, while control must use those capabilities reliably. The supplied evidence does not establish that mechanical design and software are equally important barriers. Transfer across bodies also needs separate treatment: a policy that works on one embodiment may depend on its geometry, available actions, and sensing. Separately trained policies for different configurations do not demonstrate that a single policy can transfer between them.

current_state.text: Colosseum V2 was submitted to arXiv on 26 May 2026 and revised on 29 September 2026 as version 4. According to the supplied review of its retained full paper, it evaluates 28 simulated tasks in 13 task categories across single-arm and bimanual Franka configurations. Its reported evaluations cover ACT and π0.5, with a separate multitask policy trained for each model and robot configuration, yielding four policies. This is evidence about those evaluated policies and configurations, rather than unrestricted transfer across robot bodies. The supplied record identifies an arXiv preprint; it does not establish peer-reviewed publication.

The evaluations identify robustness limitations under visual, language, and action perturbations. Effects differ by model and condition: some changes produce degradation, while others have negligible or positive effects. The supported conclusion is that strong baseline task performance does not ensure robust generalization, rather than that every perturbation reduces performance. Neither the abstract nor the retained paper, as described in the review, reports a robot completing open-ended household work.

The paper also includes hardware validation, but its scope is limited to one policy, five tasks, and seven perturbation conditions. Its simulation explicitly excludes deformable-object manipulation and several important contact effects. The demonstrated achievement is therefore a generalization benchmark, model-specific findings, and bounded hardware validation. These are useful measurement and research results, not a demonstration of the complete innovation.

The earlier research lists a purported Neurocomputing survey, “A survey on robotic manipulation of deformable objects,” as an October 2026 publication and describes its access as abstract-only. However, the supplied source index retains no document or extracted text for that URL, and the validated review could not assess its identity, publication date, or conclusions. It consequently cannot substantiate the earlier claim about the state of deformable-object manipulation. This access gap does not establish that the survey or its reported conclusion is false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material establishes dated benchmark findings through the inspected September 2026 revision, but contains no freshness record establishing coverage through 1 November 2026. No absolute household success rate is supported here. The secondary pages mentioned in the earlier research were not supplied, so neither their numerical claims nor their review status can be assessed. These limitations prevent a comprehensive present-day verdict, rather than invalidating the benchmark findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: one mobile manipulator enters an unmodified dwelling or workshop excluded from its training and completes a pre-registered set of multi-step tasks without teleoperation or demonstrations for those evaluation tasks. Examples include preparing a simple meal from a stocked kitchen, clearing and cleaning a room, and assembling an unfamiliar object from instructions. A scripted factory cell or a single simulated benchmark would not satisfy this proposed real-world milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered multi-step tasks without teleoperation or demonstrations in unseen unmodified site

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement protocol: require success on at least 90 percent of trials for each task, rather than allowing strong results on easy tasks to conceal poor results on others. Specify trial counts, task-success definitions, allowed preparation, time limits, interventions, and failure rules before testing. Report unsuccessful trials and uncertainty around success estimates. The percentage and protocol are proposals, not established standards, empirical achievements, or evidence of human-equivalent reliability.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-specified rules: at least 90 percent per-task success, uncertainty reported

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth requirements: repeat evaluation across independently selected unfamiliar settings, objects, layouts, lighting conditions, and instruction variants, with enough procedural detail for another team to reproduce the test. Practical reporting should state operating restrictions, preparation requirements, execution times, maintenance needs, and the consequences of failures. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within these conditions, not literal universality across all homes, workshops, or physical tasks.
completion_criteria.label: Independently selected unfamiliar conditions repeated reproducibly with operating limits stated

completion_criteria.text: Proposed extension to the broader goal: evaluate transfer across materially different robot bodies separately, specifying what retraining, calibration, adaptation, or additional demonstrations are allowed. Success by one mobile manipulator would establish a substantial milestone for one embodiment. It would not complete the cross-body component. Likewise, claims about deformable materials, laboratory work, or industrial operations should depend on demonstrations covering those materials and workflows.
completion_criteria.label: Separate transfer across materially different robot bodies states allowed adaptation

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with CSC-03, “Competent general machine intelligence”: general reasoning and instruction understanding could support physical autonomy, but successful physical work also requires perception, embodiment, and control under uncertain contact. CSC-08 does not require competence in every cognitive profession, and broad cognitive competence alone would not demonstrate physical autonomy. The supplied roster provides only CSC-03's title, so no more specific boundary between the entries can be established.

Conceptual comparison with CSC-06, “A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems”: both concern performance beyond training conditions. CSC-06 concerns a predictive theory; CSC-08 concerns an operational physical capability. Such a theory could help explain or design robust robot policies, but a robot demonstration would not itself establish the theory, and a theory would still require translation into effective perception and control.

Conceptual comparison with CSC-10, “Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models,” and CSC-04, “Industrial-cost proof-carrying software”: assurance methods could support confidence in components or specified behaviors of an autonomous robot. They remain distinct from demonstrating physical competence in unfamiliar settings. A software guarantee depends on its assumptions and scope, while physical task success also depends on sensing, hardware, and environmental interactions. Conversely, a high empirical success rate is not a machine-checked guarantee.

Conceptual comparison with CSC-07, “Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery”: reliable mathematical discovery is a separate capability, not a prerequisite built into this physical-autonomy goal. A system could perform useful household manipulation without discovering or proving new mathematics. These comparisons preserve the roster entries as distinct innovations; they do not imply that achieving one automatically achieves another.

change_log.change: Preserved CSC-08's identity and broad autonomy goal while separating that goal from the limitations demonstrated for particular robot policies.
change_log.reason: The benchmark supports distribution-shift failures in evaluated systems, not an exhaustive claim that every existing system lacks the capability.

change_log.change: Expanded the benchmark description to include simulated task scope, Franka configurations, ACT and π0.5, separately trained policies, and bounded hardware validation.
change_log.reason: These review-supported details distinguish benchmark breadth from cross-body policy transfer and open-ended real-world autonomy.

change_log.change: Qualified robustness findings as dependent on model and perturbation condition.
change_log.reason: The review reports negligible or positive effects in some conditions, so uniform degradation would overstate the findings.

change_log.change: Integrated rigid-body simulation limits and omitted contact phenomena into the account of remaining barriers.
change_log.reason: Deformable objects, frictional uncertainty, compliance, force feedback, and stick–slip transitions explain why benchmark results do not resolve ordinary contact-rich work.

change_log.change: Retained the survey reference with its access limitation, while withdrawing reliance on its asserted date and conclusions as established evidence.
change_log.reason: The research described abstract-only access, but no survey artifact or extracted text was retained for the validated review.

change_log.change: Removed the unsupported categorical characterization of industrial robots and the ranking of mechanical design as a co-equal barrier.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence establishes neither generalization. Hardware requirements remain part of the capability explanation.

change_log.change: Preserved the powered-flight analogy as an impact judgment and qualified downstream applications and human-reliability comparisons.
change_log.reason: The analogy is interpretive; broader applications require additional capabilities, and 90 percent trial success does not establish parity with a careful person.

change_log.change: Made the proposed 90 percent threshold per-task and added advance rules for trials, preparation, interventions, failures, reproducibility, and operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: These details make the milestone assessable without presenting a proposed protocol as an established standard or proof of universality.

change_log.change: Separated the single-embodiment milestone from cross-body evaluation and added title-bounded comparisons with relevant roster entries.
change_log.reason: Environmental generalization, embodiment transfer, cognitive competence, generalization theory, and formal assurance are overlapping but distinct goals.

change_log.change: Replaced claims of comprehensive current coverage and unsupported household rates with explicit evidence boundaries.
change_log.reason: The freshness record is empty, and the cited secondary pages and numerical claims were not supplied.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any system outside the reviewed evaluations meets the full autonomy goal.
The Neurocomputing survey's identity, publication date, and conclusions remain unassessed because no source text was retained.
Developments after the inspected 29 September 2026 revision are not covered by a supplied freshness record.
No supported absolute household success rate or human-reliability comparison is available in the supplied material.
The proposed evaluation still needs concrete trial counts, task definitions, preparation and intervention rules, time limits, and acceptable failure consequences for a particular implementation.
Cross-body generalization remains a separate evaluation question, including how much calibration, adaptation, or retraining should be permitted.
The roster supplies titles rather than full definitions for related concepts, limiting the precision of overlap comparisons.
